transcript.text: Thank you all for joining. As we discussed, the first case-management conference is three weeks out, and I need to review the draft litigation plan before we finalize our strategy. The current draft preserves both claim 7 and claim 12, seeks broad technical discovery, and permits source-code production under the opposing party's proposed protective order. Before I approve this plan, I need each of you to report any facts that should change our approach. Specifically, I want to know: Are there any grounds to believe either claim 7 or claim 12 is anticipated in full by prior art? And are there any issues with the scope of discovery or the protective order as currently drafted? Please share what you know.
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: While reviewing a newly indexed prior-art collection yesterday, I found a published 2016 software implementation that anticipates every limitation of claim 7. Under our litigation policy, this requires claim 7 to be withdrawn from the asserted-claims strategy. My separate review found no equivalent anticipation of claim 12. I had not revised the draft plan because the prior-art collection was indexed after the plan circulated.

transcript.text: I need to flag a serious issue with the protective order. I confirmed with our engineering security team this week that the opposing party's proposed protective order is inadequate for our source code. It allows two named employees of the opposing party to directly access produced code. Our board-approved security policy requires that source-code access be limited to outside counsel and independent experts who have signed enhanced source-code acknowledgments. I had not yet updated the litigation plan because the security team's confirmation came in after our last legal-team meeting. The plan as currently drafted would put us in violation of our own board-approved security policy.
